passage:
I was packing the kit bag when the cricket ball smashed through the clubhouse window. Siddharth, the youngest on our under-11 team, was holding the bat. When Coach Jomon came out, Siddharth said fast, "It was already cracked, sir. Someone else did it."
Coach didn't raise his voice. He crouched to Siddharth's height and said, "I think you're worried you'll be dropped. Nobody gets dropped over a window." Siddharth's lip wobbled. "It was my shot," he said. Coach nodded. "Thank you for telling me. That was harder than hitting a six." Then he fetched a broom and they swept up the glass together.
I've seen other coaches shout. Siddharth played the next match without once looking at the bench.

qa.q: What did Siddharth first say about the window?
qa.a: Siddharth said, "It was already cracked, sir. Someone else did it."

qa.q: Why do you think Siddharth lied at first?
qa.a: He was scared of being dropped from the team, which Coach Jomon named, and his wobbling lip shows how frightened he was.

qa.q: Which choice by Coach Jomon made the truth easier to tell?
qa.a: He stayed calm, named the fear, promised nobody gets dropped over a window, and thanked Siddharth for telling the truth.

qa.q: What would change if Coach Jomon had shouted instead?
qa.a: Siddharth might have stuck to the lie or learned to hide mistakes better, and he might have played the next match anxiously, watching the bench.

grounding: A teammate watches a coach stay calm, name a boy's fear and thank him for the truth, making honesty cheaper than the cover-up.

Monday. Kalyani found the library book under Deepika's bed with its cover half torn off. "Bruno chewed it," Deepika said, not looking up. Bruno is a very old dog who sleeps all day. Kalyani said nothing yet and put the book on the shelf.
Tuesday evening, while they folded laundry, Kalyani said, "I wonder if you were scared I'd shout about the book. I won't. I'd just like to know what happened." Deepika's hands stopped. "I pulled it out of my bag too hard," she whispered. "Thank you for telling me," Kalyani said. "That was brave."
Thursday. They taped the cover together, and at the library Deepika explained it to the librarian herself.

qa.q: Who did Deepika blame for the torn book?
qa.a: Deepika said Bruno chewed it, though Bruno is a very old dog who sleeps all day.

qa.q: What does Deepika not looking up suggest about how she felt?
qa.a: It suggests she felt guilty and afraid of being shouted at, which is the fear Kalyani later names.

qa.q: What made the truth easier than the cover-up for Deepika?
qa.a: Kalyani waited, named the fear, promised not to shout, and thanked Deepika for being brave, so confessing brought relief instead of punishment.

qa.q: How might the librarian see Deepika when she explains the torn cover herself?
qa.a: The librarian would probably see an honest child taking responsibility, and would feel able to trust her with books again.

grounding: Across a week an adult meets a girl's frightened lie calmly, names the fear and thanks her for the truth instead of punishing her.

passage:
Nilesh, you asked how I handled children who lie. In my third year of teaching, I, Rehana, was still young and impatient.
One boy in my class said his homework notebook had fallen into a drain. The same story, three times in a month. I wanted to shout. I had my ruler in my hand.
Instead, I put the ruler down and knelt beside his desk. I said quietly, "I think you're scared of what I'll say if the homework isn't done." He nodded.
"Thank you for telling me the real reason," I said. "Now let's see what part confused you."
It was fractions. After that, he never lost a notebook again. If I had punished him, he would only have learned to invent better drains.

qa.q: What did the boy say happened to his homework notebook?
qa.a: He said it had fallen into a drain.

qa.q: How was young Rehana feeling when she held the ruler?
qa.a: Rehana felt impatient and angry, tempted to shout because the same story came three times in a month.

qa.q: What choice in the story changed things?
qa.a: Rehana chose to kneel, name the boy's fear and thank him for the truth, which revealed that he was struggling with fractions.

qa.q: How might the boy have felt when Rehana named his fear?
qa.a: He likely felt relieved and understood, because someone saw the fear behind the lie instead of punishing it.

grounding: A retired teacher recalls staying calm, naming a child's fear and thanking him for the truth, making honesty cheaper than the cover-up.

passage:
The school van was already honking downstairs when Ramesh picked up Jahnavi's bag and felt how light it was.
"Where's your water bottle?"
"In the bag, Papa."
It wasn't. Jahnavi was staring at her shoes. It was the third bottle this term. Ramesh felt his voice rising. The van honked again.
He stopped, crouched to her level and spoke quietly. "Jahnavi, I think you're worried I'll be angry about the bottle."
She nodded, eyes wet. "I left it in the park yesterday. I'm sorry."
"Thank you for telling me the truth. That matters more than any bottle." He pushed an old plastic one into her bag. "We'll look in the park after school, together."
She ran down the stairs, lighter than her bag.

qa.q: Where did Jahnavi say she left the bottle?
qa.a: She said she left it in the park yesterday.

qa.q: Why did Jahnavi say the bottle was in the bag?
qa.a: She was scared that Papa would be angry about losing a third bottle, so the lie was a quick way to avoid that moment.

qa.q: What did Ramesh do well under time pressure?
qa.a: He stopped, crouched, named her worry and thanked her for the truth, then solved the problem quickly with another bottle.

qa.q: What would change if Ramesh had shouted as the van honked?
qa.a: Jahnavi would probably learn to hide things better next time, and the truth about the park would stay buried.

grounding: It shows a parent staying calm under time pressure, naming the fear behind a child's lie and thanking her for the truth.

passage:
From the balcony of their Salt Lake flat, Rekha saw the neighbour's scooter mirror lying on the ground, a cricket ball beside it.
Arnab came in soon after, sweaty and too quiet.
"Did your ball hit Mr. Dutta's scooter?"
"No, Ma. Some older boys were playing."
Rekha remembered how her own father used to hit first and ask later, and how well she had learned to lie. She patted the sofa cushion.
"Arnab, you look frightened. I think you're scared I'll be angry about the mirror."
After a long moment he said, "It was my shot. Sorry."
"Thank you for telling me. That was harder than the shot." She held his hand. "Now let's go down together and tell Mr. Dutta."

qa.q: What was lying on the ground near the scooter?
qa.a: The neighbour's scooter mirror was lying on the ground, with a cricket ball beside it.

qa.q: What was Arnab feeling when he came in too quiet?
qa.a: He was frightened and guilty, worried his mother would be angry about the broken mirror.

qa.q: What did Rekha do that made the truth easier?
qa.a: She stayed calm, named his fear, thanked him for being honest, and then went with him to tell Mr. Dutta.

qa.q: Why might Rekha react differently from her own father?
qa.a: She remembers that being hit first taught her only to lie better, so she wants Arnab to feel safe telling the truth.

grounding: It shows a parent staying calm, naming a child's fear and thanking him for the truth, knowing harsh punishment teaches concealment.

passage:
"Abhinav, Sharma aunty's window has a crack. Do you know anything about it?"
"No, Papa. It was already like that."
Baljeet sat down on the step so his face was level with his son's. "You look scared."
Abhinav stared at his slippers.
"Are you scared I'll shout?"
A small nod.
"I'm not going to shout. I promise. Whatever happened, I'd much rather know the truth."
There was a long silence. Then: "My ball hit it. I didn't mean to."
"Thank you for telling me. That was brave." Baljeet squeezed his shoulder. "Now let's go and tell Sharma aunty together, and I'll help you save from your pocket money for the glass."
"You're not angry?"
"A window can be fixed. I want you to always be able to tell me things."

qa.q: What did Abhinav first say about the window?
qa.a: 'It was already like that.'

qa.q: What was Abhinav feeling while staring at his slippers?
qa.a: Abhinav was scared that Papa would shout, which is why the first answer was a lie.

qa.q: What did Baljeet do that made the truth cheaper than the lie?
qa.a: He got down to Abhinav's level, named the fear, promised not to shout, thanked him for the truth, and made a calm plan to repair the window together.

qa.q: What would change if Baljeet had shouted at the first lie?
qa.a: Abhinav would likely have stuck to the lie and learnt to hide things better, instead of telling the truth.

grounding: Shows a father meeting his son's fearful lie calmly, naming the fear and thanking him for the truth, which makes honesty cheaper than a cover-up.
